description: Coaxial 30x AFOCAL three-mirror telescope, first-order regression fixture. Transcribed from J.M. Rodgers' CODE V deck CentAfo_Coaxial_OnAxisFOV (2026-08-02, see mmacos/design/rodgers2/PACKET.md) and re-derived paraxially rather than quoted. The point of the fixture is that BOTH first-order conditions of an afocal telescope close on it simultaneously: the marginal ray leaves parallel (afocal), and the chief ray images the stop onto a plane a specified distance past the last mirror (the interface pupil). A focal fixture cannot test either.
convention: Unfolded thin-lens equivalent; mirror f = R/2 with a CONVEX mirror a negative lens; R given as MAGNITUDES with a separate convex flag (the MACOS emission convention: KrElt = -|R| for every mirror, concave vs convex is geometry). Metres. Marginal ray: collimated, full aperture, launched at M1. Chief ray: unit field angle through the stop, which sits 50 mm AHEAD of M1 -- that offset is carried, not approximated away, because it is what makes the entrance pupil not simply be M1.

expected_first_order.u_out_note: the afocal condition; 0 by design, the 3 urad residual is his real-ray tuning of R3

independent_witness.note: His coldstop station was placed by hand in CODE V and is not an input to anything above. That the paraxial exit pupil lands 0.8 mm from it, on a 33 mm beam, is the check that the transcription, the sign conventions and the paraxial model all agree.

how_to_use.assert: afocal_first_order(R, t, convex, 'D', 1.0, 'stop_ahead', 0.050) must reproduce every entry of expected_first_order to 1e-6 relative.
how_to_use.gate: STOP AND FIX -- never widen. A drift here means the paraxial model, the convex-flag convention, or the stop handling has changed, and every afocal layout closed against it is wrong by the same amount.

caution.which_variant: Use the ON-AXIS variant, as here. His S3/S4 re-solves moved R3 by 3.8% to recollimate the REAL marginal ray at f/1.25; paraxially they leave 41 urad of convergence and a 4.8% small exit beam. Both are correct answers to different questions, but seeding a first-order study from S3 builds a 31.4x telescope.
